title: Rate limiter for a public API
like: the limits on a public API like GitHub's
brief: Developers call your public API from scripts and apps. A few misbehaving or malicious clients can crowd out everyone else. Build limits that are fair, fast and cheap, and that survive a retry storm.

clarify.q: What should an over-limit client see?
clarify.a: A quick, polite "429 slow down" with a hint when to try again. It must be faster than a normal answer.

clarify.q: Is the limit per person or per key?
clarify.a: Per API key. One customer may have many servers sharing one key.

clarify.q: If the limiter itself breaks, do we let traffic through or block it?
clarify.a: Let it through for ordinary traffic. A broken limiter must not take the whole API down. Abuse protection is still wanted.

clarify.q: How exact must the counting be?
clarify.a: Close is fine. Being off by a few percent is acceptable.

notes: Estimate memory for 2 million counters at about 100 bytes per key, including overhead.
Typical limit: 5,000 requests an hour per key, bursts allowed (approx.).

numbers.label: Counter memory for 2 million keys at 100 bytes each (approx.)
Limit check cost
numbers.how: One in-memory counter update, about the speed of a cache hit (approx.)

hints: Where is the cheapest place to say no: before your servers do any work, or after?
Add a rate limiter in front of the gateway so abusive keys are stopped early. Think about who else is flooding you in the retry storm.
Users, WAF, rate limiter, API gateway, servers, cache, key-value store. Set the limiter fail-open and a sensible per-client limit.

editorial.summary: Count requests per key in fast memory and refuse the extra ones before they reach the expensive part. Abusive traffic and retry storms get stopped at the door, while ordinary clients never notice the limiter.

designs.name: Limiter in front of the gateway
designs.why: A WAF removes obvious junk, the limiter applies the per-key limit, and only legitimate traffic reaches the servers. Failing open keeps the API up if the limiter breaks.

designs.name: Limit at the gateway only
designs.why: Use the gateway's own per-key throttle. Fewer parts and lower cost, but it cannot share counters across regions or cap retries as sharply.

tradeoffs: Fail-open keeps users happy when the limiter breaks, but briefly lets abusers through. Fail-closed is safer for abuse, riskier for uptime.
A shared counter is exact but adds a network hop. Local counters are fastest but let a key exceed the limit across many servers.
Retries multiply load. A good limiter also caps how many retries a client may send.
Per-key limits protect against one customer. A WAF stops junk that is not tied to any key at all.
editorial.realWorld: Public APIs commonly allow around 1,000 to 5,000 requests an hour per key, with short bursts allowed. Limit checks are in-memory counters taking well under a millisecond (approx.).

correctness.prompt: Rate limiter for a public API: The same request is delivered twice, and a worker can crash after saving it. What uniqueness constraint and transaction would keep one durable result?
correctness.discussion: Choose a stable business operation id and enforce a unique constraint in the authoritative store. Insert the id, apply the change and save its result in one transaction. A retry returns that result. Recording the id before the change can lose work after a crash; recording it afterwards can apply the change twice. If work continues through a queue, commit an outbox entry in the same transaction and deduplicate at each consumer.

fields.label: The server commits a change, then crashes before replying. The client retries. What happens?
options: Commit the operation id, effect and result atomically; return that result on retry
Record the id first, then apply the change in a separate write
fields.explanation: Recording the id separately can either lose an operation or apply it twice. The effect and deduplication result must commit together.

fields.label: The server acknowledges a write just before its storage fails. Which evidence meets the stated recovery point?
options: A queued backup request with no completed durable copy
A measured replication or backup gap of at most 60 seconds, with a tested replay plan
fields.explanation: A scheduled copy is not a completed copy. Match acknowledgement and recovery to the stated loss boundary.
